explanation: Many silent films ended in an exciting chase, and scripts used 'cut to chase' to jump straight to it. The phrase appears in print in a 1929 novel about Hollywood.

claims.text: 'Cut to the chase' comes from film-making, where cutting to the chase scene meant skipping to the action.
The phrase does not come from fox hunting, horse racing or journalism.
Many silent comedies and adventure films ended with a chase scene.
The phrase 'cut to chase' appears in J. P. McEvoy's 1929 novel Hollywood Girl.

writerNotes: Counterintuitive: chase suggests hunting, so fox hunting is the obvious pick and is wrong. Self-check (CONTENT_GUIDE 9.3), all eleven codes confirmed true.
